episodes.209540: Increasing theta-e, steep mid level lapse rates, strong shear and limited MUCAPE allowed for the development of several thunderstorms which moved from White county to northern portions of Allen county during the morning hours. Additional storms developed in the afternoon. Low freezing levels and the elements noted above resulted in efficient hail producing storms, with one in particular leaving a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path. A few severe level hail stones were reported.
episodes.209907: A frontal boundary sank into the area on the 19th of February and then remained in the vicinity as a low-pressure system moved northeast into the Great Lakes region. The boundary became occluded overhead before being ushered northeast out of the area by the parent low on the 20th. Meanwhile, a cold front approached from the west and then washed out as it moved through the middle Ohio Valley later in the day. The first round of precipitation lifted north across West Virginia the morning of the 19th, then rounds of more robust showers and thunderstorms rolled through the area that afternoon into the night. After a very brief break in activity, more showers and storms spread into the area from the southwest shortly after midnight and then slid east across the mountains by mid-morning on the 20th. Drier conditions then took hold for the rest of the day.||Strong to severe storms downed multiple trees and power lines, and produced hail between one and one-and-three-quarter inches in size. While rainfall amounts of two inches or less were observed across much of the area, portions of the southern coal fields received two to three and a half inches. Excessive rainfall caused flooding on some roads as local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers exceeded their banks in Boone and Logan Counties. A combination of rainfall and snowmelt also prompted minor flooding on Mill Creek in Randolph County.
episodes.210329: Isolated thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the early morning hours of February 19th producing large hail.
episodes.210698: A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.
episodes.210924: As a low pressure system moved across the upper Midwest, a cold front advanced into Illinois and interacted with elevated instability. This led to scattered thunderstorms, one of which produced quarter-sized hail in Champaign County.
episodes.210938: A surface low lifted northeastward across Missouri towards the Illinois-Iowa border during the afternoon and evening of February 19th. A warm front extended east from the low into southeast Illinois. In response to this system, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed across central and southeast Illinois, with the greatest coverage being in the general vicinity of the I-70 corridor. Environmental conditions supported all severe hazards, including large hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter, damaging winds, and tornadoes, with a total of eight tornadoes occurring in the NWS Lincoln coverage area. Most of these tornadoes were brief, and none were stronger than EF-1, but one serious injury occurred in Crawford County as a result of a tornado. Another indirect injury occurred on I-57 in Effingham County when thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident.
episodes.210944: Ahead of an approaching surface low with a trailing cold front, southern winds brought warmer temperatures and moisture into southern Indiana. Highs reached into the 60s with dew points in the upper 50s. This helped to generate enough instability to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms. One of these storms dropped severe hail in Harrison County.
episodes.210945: Ahead of an approaching surface low with a trailing cold front, southern winds brought warmer temperatures and moisture into central Kentucky. Highs temperatures and dew points reached into the 60s. This helped to generate enough instability to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms. A couple of these storms dropped severe hail in Nelson and Fayette Counties.
episodes.210952: On the evening of February 18th, a thunderstorm developed over Lake Erie and tracked southeast onshore across southern Erie County. As the thunderstorm tracked onshore it strengthened and briefly became severe. The combination of favorable mid-level lapse rates, low freezing levels and shear allowed the storm to strengthen enough to produce one inch hail in Angola. After producing the hail, the storm quickly weakened as it continued to track across Erie County.
episodes.211234: A warm front approaching from the south initiated convection and resulted in a round of scattered showers and thunderstorms moving northward from northern WV to the I-70 corridor. Model soundings suggested overall weak convection, however, one overperforming cell that had rotation along the warm front resulted in several reports of hail in the relatively low CAPE environment, with the largest observed being one inch.
episodes.211256: The St. Louis forecast area was within an open warm sector during the afternoon of February 19th. Moisture and warm air advection resulted in increased instability, and multi-cell clusters fired off in south-central IL. One of these thunderstorms produced severe hail in Bond and Fayette counties.
episodes.211361: A dynamic storm system brought unseasonably warm temperatures and rounds of severe weather to eastern Kentucky on February 19th and 20th. Near record warmth, combined with intense wind shear, fueled both discrete supercells and a subsequent overnight line of showers and thunderstorms.||The primary threat focused along the Mountain Parkway corridor during the afternoon of the 19th, where thunderstorms produced up to quarter-sized hail (1.00). As the system's cold front crossed the region overnight, the threat transitioned to isolated damaging winds. High-momentum air mixing to the surface downed trees and utility lines in Lee and Breathitt counties.
episodes.211417: A series of low pressure systems moved over southern California during the mid part of the month of February, bringing heavy rain and thunderstorms, strong and gusty winds, and high elevation snow from the 10th thru the 11th, and then again on the 16th thru 18th. This resulted in a few reports of damage due to strong winds from thunderstorms. There were also several reports of flooding/flash flooding due to heavy rain.
episodes.211470: Thunderstorms along the M-59 corridor produced several hail reports, with sizes up to 1.25 inches in diameter.
episodes.211492: By mid-February, higher moisture content from a lingering front and locally induced afternoon shower and thunderstorm activity produced periods of heavy rainfall across Puerto Rico.

events.narrative: Broadcast media through social media reported that heavy rainfall resulted in water flowing over the roadway at the entrance to PR-328 toward Rayo Guaras in Sabana Grande. The flooding created hazardous driving conditions.

The 911 call center reported that emergency managers responded to flooding at the intersection of PR-317 and PR-114 in San German. Floodwaters inundated the roadway, resulting in persons stranded in at least one vehicle.

Flooding was reported in the Las Guaras sector of Sabana Grande near the municipal boundary with Lajas. Heavy runoff caused muddy water to flow rapidly over roadways, creating hazardous driving conditions.
Hail was covering the road.

County Fire reports a tree went through a roof on dawn drive. Estimated wind gusts in  the area near 50-55 mph.

A brief tornado was confirmed via storm chaser video. No damage occurred, so an intensity rating could not be assigned.
Thunderstorm winds contributed to a multi-vehicle accident on I-57 southwest of Watson, resulting in one indirect injury.
Local dispatch reported approximately quarter-sized (1.00 inch) hail in the Campton area.
A social media user located about a mile south of Hazel Green reported approximately quarter-sized (1.00 inch) hailstones.
A social media user reported a tree blown down onto a road about 1 mile west northwest of the Bethany community.

Video from a storm chaser showed a tornado develop about one mile southeast of Wheeler. The tornado caused minor damage to trees as it travelled northeast across Highway 33 before dissipating just east of N 500th St.
The local highway department reported that a tree had been blown down onto powerlines between MM10 and MM12 along KY-1812.

A short-lived tornado developed in a field three miles southwest of Yale. It moved northeast and dissipated shortly after crossing N 1675 St. The tornado resulted in tall field grass being blown over and matted down.

Storm chaser video showed a well-defined funnel cloud extending at least half way to the ground approximately four miles west of Chauncey. However, no evidence of a tornado was found in this area. This thunderstorm went on to produce a tornado in Crawford County four minutes after this funnel cloud was sighted.
A storm chaser provided video of a brief tornado occurring at this location. No damage occurred, so an intensity rating could not be assigned.

The tornado began about three miles southeast of Hardinville, where it damaged several trees near the intersection of East 350th Avenue and North 825th Street. It then intensified to EF-1 as it moved northeast, severely damaging two homes including one mobile home that was thrown off its foundation and wrapped around a tree. An elderly woman in that mobile home was hospitalized with serious injuries. The tornado continued northeast, crossing several tree lines and damaging additional homes and farm buildings along 1125th Street and East 465th Avenue. After that, the tornado only produced minor tree damage. It eventually crossed State Highway 1 and dissipated about 2.5 miles north-northeast of Flat Rock.
A storm chaser provided video of a brief tornado occurring in an open field. No damage occurred, so an intensity rating could not be assigned.

An EF-0 tornado tracked 4.10 miles over southern Sullivan County, between the Paxton and Carlisle communities. The maximum path width was 300 yards with multiple outbuildings significantly or completely destroyed and damage to trees.  The supercell originally spawned two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, which lifted before crossing the Wabash River into southwestern Sullivan County near Indiana Route 58. The tornado appeared to frequently come in contact with the ground at a few locations east of Route 58 but never remained in contact with the ground for a long distance, yet demonstrated damage that reflects high-end EF0 winds around 80 mph. The tornado maintained EF-0 intensity as it moved east-northeast through agricultural land, snapping a mix of large hardwood and softwood trees before lifting from Sullivan County. Damage was observed just northwest of Carlisle, where several small outbuildings sustained major damage. In this location, wind speeds were estimated at 80 mph, consistent with EF-0 intensity. The tornado continued across US-41 just south of Paxton, where the strongest damage, an additional outbuilding completely destroyed along with several large trees knocked over and snapped, was consistent with winds upwards of 85 mph;  the storm survey estimates that the width of the tree damage spanned around 300 yards in an adjacent field.  Peak wind speeds were estimated at 85 mph.
Thunderstorm wind gusts downed a large tree onto a car.
Hail up to 1.25 inches also reported in village of Hoosier.
Several power poles were pushed over, but not completely toppled by thunderstorm wind gusts.

An EF-2 tornado tracked 3.73 miles through west-central Monroe County, across the Bloomington Airport up to the Interstate Route 69 interchange with Indiana Route 48.  The maximum path width was 440 yards with the tornado causing significant damage to neighborhoods, apartments, businesses, and portions of the airport. Extensive tree damage also occurred.||The tornado first developed in wooded areas west of the airport before rapidly intensifying as it moved into a small neighborhood just west of the airport. This area experienced the event's most intense winds, extensive tree damage along with multiple points of structural damage to homes.  As the tornado progressed eastward, it caused damage to an airplane hangar.  While passing over the airfield, the KBMG ASOS recorded a wind gust of 70 mph.  The tornado continued east-northeast, damaging numerous homes before striking a newly constructed neighborhood where additional high-end EF-1 to low-end EF-2 damage occurred. Additional EF-1 damage was observed further northeast at an apartment complex. After producing damage to a bank overhang and causing roofing damage to several warehouse structures, the tornado dissipated near the east end of this business district, immediately west of I-69.  Peak wind speeds were estimated at 120 mph.
